column1: What is schema drift in a SQL database project workflow?
column2:
Differences between the project's intended schema and the live database schema.
Drift means the actual database no longer matches the intended schema. For example, an emergency column addition in production can leave the live table different from its committed definition.
Review source

column1: What commonly introduces schema drift outside a database deployment pipeline?
column2:
Manual changes, unrecorded emergency hotfixes, or third-party schema modifications.
A change made outside the normal release path can reach the database without updating the project. For example, an application migration can add an index the project does not define.
Review source

column1: In Schema Compare, which side receives the proposed updates?
column2:
The target is updated to match the source.
The source is the desired state for this comparison. The target receives the proposed changes. You can compare against a DACPAC as target, but you cannot update that package in place.
Review source

column1: After detecting an unexpected schema difference, what decision tells you whether to change the project or the live database?
column2:
Which differences belong in the intended database schema.
Decide whether each difference is an approved change to keep or an unwanted change to reverse. That decision tells you whether the project or the live database needs an update.
Review source

column1: An approved hotfix exists only in production. How do you bring that change into the SQL project?
column2:
Compare database to project and import the selected differences.
Set the live database as the source and the project as the target. Select the hotfix changes you intend to preserve. Commit them so the next build includes those definitions.
Review source

column1: The SQL project is correct but production drifted. How do you bring the live schema back into line?
column2:
Review and deploy the changes needed to restore the project's intended schema.
Use the project or its DACPAC as the desired state and the live database as the target. Review the proposed changes before applying them, especially if restoring the definition can remove data.
Review source

column1: Why can a schema comparison miss differences that actually exist?
column2:
Its ignore settings or excluded object types can hide them.
Comparison settings define what counts as a reported difference. For example, excluded indexes can differ even when the tool finds no changes. Record the settings so later runs cover the same scope.
Review source

column1: Where do you write SqlPackage Extract output to avoid replacing the team's checked-in project files?
column2:
A separate output path outside the maintained project.
Write the extraction to a new folder, then compare it with the project. OverwriteFiles defaults to True, so using the maintained source folder can overwrite existing files.
Review source

column1: Why can Git report a changed SQL file even when the database schema has not changed?
column2:
File changes do not map one-to-one to meaningful schema differences.
A file diff measures text changes, not database objects. Reformatting one definition can show up in Git without changing the schema. Compare the schema models when you need meaningful database differences.
Review source

column1: What SqlPackage output can a pipeline inspect for planned drops or table rebuilds before publishing?
column2:
Inspect operations in the generated XML deployment report.
DeployReport lists operations that a publish would perform for the chosen target. A pipeline can require approval when the report includes a drop or rebuild, before publishing any changes.
Review source

column1: Which tool checks whether two .dacpac build artifacts remain equivalent after project-format conversion?
column2:
DacpacVerify.
DacpacVerify checks more than object definitions. It also checks package content such as deployment scripts and SQLCMD variables. That helps catch a conversion that preserves the schema but drops a seed script.
Review source

column1: Which schema does SqlPackage DriftReport compare the live database against?
column2:
The database's last registered schema, not an arbitrary SQL project.
DriftReport compares the live schema with the database's registration baseline. It does not use a newly built DACPAC as its baseline. Use DeployReport for changes needed to publish a particular build.
Review source

column1: Why can a table rebuild be risky even if the deployment copies all the rows into the replacement table?
column2:
Rebuilding a table can have a significant performance impact.
A rebuild can copy rows into a replacement table and hold locks while it works. Data can survive while the deployment still takes longer or interrupts workload access.
Review source

column1: By default, what does SqlPackage Extract capture from a live database?
column2:
The database schema.
By default, Extract captures object definitions without copying table rows. Two databases can have identical definitions but different lookup values. Compare their data separately if that is what you need to detect.
Review source
